title: Use the customer's task vocabulary
trigger: The site describes familiar work with internal product jargon that prospects do not use.
action: Replace internal labels in the main explanation with terms found in actual customer questions, search queries or support conversations. Keep necessary product names, but connect them to the recognizable task the first time they appear.
mechanism: Familiar language may reduce translation effort and make the offer easier to recognize.
guardrail: Use research as vocabulary evidence, not fabricated customer quotations; confirm that simpler wording preserves meaning.
measure: Offer comprehension and qualified paid conversion; terminology confusion.

title: Replace praise with observable verbs
trigger: Descriptions rely on words such as powerful, effortless or revolutionary without explaining behavior.
action: Rewrite each central claim as something the customer can observe the product doing, such as grouping duplicate requests or exporting an approved report. Retain a short explanation of why that action matters to the buyer's work.
mechanism: Specific actions may be easier to evaluate than promotional adjectives.
guardrail: Demonstrate the named behavior in the current product; avoid turning a potential benefit into a guaranteed result.
measure: Paid activation into the stated capability; expectation mismatch.

title: Attach the condition to the benefit
trigger: A headline benefit is true only for some workloads, but its necessary condition appears far away.
action: Put the material condition next to the benefit in plain language, such as explaining that a workflow needs a supported data source. Preserve an appealing main statement while making it clear when that statement applies.
mechanism: Conditional specificity may make a claim more credible and help buyers assess fit.
guardrail: Identify conditions from actual product behavior; do not use tiny qualifiers to rescue an otherwise misleading headline.
measure: Qualified purchases; condition-related refunds.

title: Use a concrete before-and-after sentence
trigger: A feature list leaves visitors to infer how their everyday work would change.
action: Write one concise before-and-after comparison using a real task: describe the current repeated step, then the supported new workflow. Keep the comparison on the same task and outcome rather than switching to a more favorable example.
mechanism: A contrast in recognizable work may make the benefit easier to mentally simulate.
guardrail: Verify both workflows and include required review or setup; do not invent customer time savings.
measure: Benefit comprehension and paid conversion; workflow mismatch.

title: Frame an evidenced cost of delay
trigger: The product solves a costly recurring problem, but the page describes only optional convenience.
action: Explain the documented consequence of leaving that problem unresolved, such as requests remaining unassigned or reports becoming outdated. Pair the consequence with the actual supported remedy so the buyer can judge whether action matters now.
mechanism: A concrete loss frame may make an existing problem more salient.
guardrail: Use verified consequences or explicitly labeled assumptions; avoid fear, invented financial losses and unsupported personal claims.
measure: Qualified purchases; anxiety or misleading-claim complaints.

title: Offer an attainable gain frame
trigger: The page repeatedly emphasizes mistakes and failure, while buyers struggle to picture a useful positive outcome.
action: Rewrite a central explanation around the achievable benefit of the supported workflow, such as knowing which request needs attention. Keep material risk information available, but let the main story show what better operation looks like.
mechanism: An attainable gain may make starting feel constructive rather than threatening.
guardrail: Do not imply guaranteed success or conceal the effort needed; compare outcome quality, not merely copy preference.
measure: Paid activation; disappointment and avoidance-related exits.

title: Let buyers picture the first ordinary day
trigger: The marketing remains abstract even after visitors understand the feature names.
action: Describe a short, realistic sequence of using the product during an ordinary workday: what arrives, what the person sees, what they decide and what happens next. Use actual interface behavior and preserve any manual work.
mechanism: Mental simulation may help a buyer connect features to personal use.
guardrail: Label the sequence as an example; avoid unsupported timing, automation or lifestyle promises.
measure: Use-case comprehension and paid activation; expectation mismatch.

title: Translate an abstract unit with arithmetic
trigger: The offer uses requests, credits or operations that buyers cannot map to a recognizable task.
action: Add a worked example with explicit assumptions, such as ten items using three operations each consuming thirty operations. Keep the actual unit as the entitlement and explain which additional actions can consume more, so the example remains conditional.
mechanism: Concrete quantities may make an unfamiliar value metric easier to evaluate.
guardrail: Use the real counting rule; do not present example task counts as guaranteed completed outcomes.
measure: Plan-fit purchases; allowance confusion and early exhaustion.

title: Use a bounded explanatory analogy
trigger: A novel product category is difficult to explain because visitors lack a familiar frame of reference.
action: Introduce one accurate analogy, such as an inbox for incoming requests, then name the important differences and real behavior. Use the analogy to orient the buyer before presenting precise features, rather than asking them to understand a newly invented category name.
mechanism: A familiar conceptual structure may reduce the effort of understanding an unfamiliar product.
guardrail: Choose an analogy that preserves the relevant relationships; explicitly correct likely false inferences and avoid suggesting nonexistent capabilities.
measure: Product comprehension and qualified paid conversion; analogy-driven misconceptions.

title: Keep qualifications beside numeric claims
trigger: A strong number appears in the main copy while its population, period or scope is hidden elsewhere.
action: Attach the essential qualifier to the number in readable nearby text, such as the measured task, timeframe or relevant customer segment. Link fuller methodology separately, retaining enough local context to understand the claim correctly.
mechanism: An interpretable number may feel more credible and prevent an overly broad inference.
guardrail: Use the actual evidence and denominator; do not imply typical results from a selected exceptional case.
measure: Qualified paid conversion; claim-comprehension errors.

title: Connect features through a consequence chain
trigger: Copy lists capabilities and then adds generic benefits that do not logically follow.
action: For a decisive capability, write the short chain from product action to workflow consequence to buyer benefit. For example, assigned ownership can make unanswered work visible; avoid jumping directly from a feature to guaranteed revenue growth.
mechanism: A coherent explanation may reduce the reasoning the buyer must supply.
guardrail: Stop the chain where evidence stops; distinguish a supported function from an expected business outcome.
measure: Paid adoption of the capability; benefit-related disappointment.

title: Make headings answer buying questions
trigger: Section headings such as features, solutions or benefits provide little information when scanned.
action: Replace generic headings with concise answers to the actual question handled by that section, such as how shared work is reviewed or which inputs are supported. Ensure the section delivers on the heading before adding persuasive wording.
mechanism: Information-bearing headings may help scanners find decisive evidence more quickly.
guardrail: Do not turn every heading into an unsupported claim; preserve clear page structure and accessibility.
measure: Qualified progression to purchase; missed-information support.

title: Explain necessary jargon at first use
trigger: A technical term is essential to the product but unfamiliar to a substantial part of the buying audience.
action: Keep the accurate term and add a short plain-language explanation at its first meaningful use. Offer deeper documentation for specialists rather than making beginners decode an acronym or forcing experts through a long primer.
mechanism: A dual-level explanation may reduce comprehension effort without sacrificing precision.
guardrail: Have the explanation preserve the technical meaning; do not oversimplify security, billing or compatibility constraints.
measure: Comprehension and paid conversion; technical misunderstanding.

title: Use parallel wording for comparable choices
trigger: Equivalent attributes use mixed grammatical forms, forcing buyers to interpret the wording before they can compare the offers.
action: Rewrite comparable descriptions in parallel grammar and units, such as action verb plus object for each capability. Keep equivalent conditions in the same sentence position so readers can compare meaning without translating between slogans, nouns and technical labels.
mechanism: Linguistic consistency may reduce the mental effort needed to distinguish real differences.
guardrail: Preserve actual capability and limitations; do not make unequal features sound equivalent or remove necessary qualifications.
measure: Correct plan comprehension and qualified paid conversion; mistaken feature expectations.

title: Put the direct answer before explanation
trigger: Important FAQ answers begin with several sentences of context before revealing whether the product fits.
action: Start with the precise answer, then explain the condition or exception and link any necessary detail. For example, say which file types work before discussing the import architecture, so the reader can decide whether to continue.
mechanism: Reduced search effort may help hesitant buyers resolve specific doubts.
guardrail: Avoid an absolute yes or no when the actual answer is conditional; keep the qualification in the same visible answer.
measure: Qualified purchase completion; repeated unanswered questions.

title: Use ranges for variable measured outcomes
trigger: A single outcome number gives a false impression of precision because customer workloads vary widely.
action: When suitable measurements exist, show an interpretable range or distribution with its task and population instead of an unsupported universal figure. Explain the main drivers of variation and keep exceptional examples labeled as such.
mechanism: Calibrated expectations may make evidence more believable and reduce regret.
guardrail: Do not invent a range or present it as guaranteed coverage; ensure the chosen summary represents the underlying data.
measure: Qualified purchases; outcome-expectation complaints.

title: Keep one name for each concept
trigger: The same object is called a workspace, project, board and account across marketing pages.
action: Create a short terminology map and use one primary name for each distinct concept throughout the buying journey. Introduce a necessary synonym once, then maintain the distinction between objects rather than using stylistic variation.
mechanism: Consistent labels may reduce mental bookkeeping and mistaken assumptions.
guardrail: Confirm that the concepts truly match; do not merge different permissions, entitlements or account levels for simpler copy.
measure: Purchase completion; terminology-related support.

title: Name the actor in important promises
trigger: Sentences such as 'it is checked' or 'everything gets updated' leave buyers unsure who performs the work.
action: Rewrite consequential statements with an explicit actor: the user, the software, a teammate or the support team. Name any approval step and its owner, particularly where an automatic-sounding phrase currently hides manual effort.
mechanism: Agency clarity may help buyers estimate effort and trust the promise.
guardrail: Verify responsibilities against the real workflow; do not assign work or service commitments that are not provided.
measure: Qualified paid activation; responsibility misunderstandings.

title: Remove double negatives from conditions
trigger: An eligibility rule or limitation contains nested negatives that make its meaning hard to follow.
action: Rewrite the condition as a direct positive statement or a simple exclusion, then give one accurate example if needed. Preserve the original commercial meaning and ask a reviewer to explain the rule back without seeing the original.
mechanism: Linguistic fluency may reduce errors in understanding a purchase condition.
guardrail: Have the product owner verify that the rewritten condition is equivalent; do not simplify away an exception.
measure: Condition comprehension; incorrect purchases and support.

title: Localize the task rather than idioms
trigger: Translated pages preserve slogans and wordplay that obscure the actual task for another language audience.
action: Replace difficult idioms with natural task language reviewed by a competent speaker. Keep the claim, qualifications and feature scope equivalent, while allowing sentence structure and examples to match the audience's ordinary usage.
mechanism: Natural wording may reduce friction caused by decoding a foreign marketing convention.
guardrail: Verify material terms and avoid cultural stereotypes; do not imply product-language support beyond what exists.
measure: Qualified conversion in the supported locale; translation confusion.
